tasks.title: Station recon panorama
tasks.stands_for: Mastcam-Z, the stereo zoom cameras on the mast
tasks.why: You cannot describe a rock you never framed. The panorama is the record every later step is tied to.
tasks.where: Stand still at the station pin, on the flattest ground within about 5 m.
steps: Put the scale bar (or your own boot, 30 cm) in view and note which way is north.
Shoot a full circle of overlapping photos from one spot, about 20 degrees apart, held level.
Shoot the same circle again one pace to the right, so the pair is stereo and gives depth.
Say out loud and write down: station number, time on the EVA clock, what the ground is made of.
tasks.source: Bell et al. 2021, Mastcam-Z; Farley et al. 2020, Mars 2020 mission overview.
tasks.gap: The record every later step hangs on
tasks.task: Station recon panorama (5 min) - Mastcam-Z, the stereo zoom cameras on the mast

tasks.title: Remote triage of three targets
tasks.stands_for: SuperCam, laser spectroscopy from a distance (out to roughly 7 m)
tasks.why: Decide which few rocks are worth touching before spending suit time on any of them.
tasks.where: Pick three rocks 2 to 7 m away that differ: one bedrock face, one loose rock, one dusty patch.
steps: Number the three targets in the panorama and photograph each one zoomed in.
For each: note grain size, colour, layering, and whether it is in place or loose.
Rank them for the next protocol. In place beats loose; a fresh face beats a dusty one.
Write down the one you rejected and why. A rejection is data too.
tasks.source: Wiens et al. 2021 and Maurice et al. 2021, SuperCam.
tasks.gap: The record every later step hangs on
tasks.task: Remote triage of three targets (4 min) - SuperCam, laser spectroscopy from a distance (out to roughly 7 m)

tasks.title: Abrade a patch and look inside
tasks.stands_for: the abrading bit with WATSON and SHERLOC (close-up camera, deep-UV Raman and fluorescence)
tasks.why: Mars is covered in dust and a weathered rind. The real rock starts a few millimetres down.
tasks.where: On bedrock still attached to the ground, on a face you can reach standing up.
steps: Brush the dust off a patch about the size of your palm.
Grind a flat patch about 5 cm across and a few mm deep, the size Perseverance makes.
Photograph the patch close up, filling the frame, with the scale bar touching it.
Describe the fresh surface: grain size, cement between grains, veins, how it differs from the rind.
Shade the patch with your body and look for anything that glows. That is the organics check.
tasks.source: Bhartia et al. 2021, SHERLOC; Mars 2020 abrasion patches are about 5 cm across.
tasks.signal: No rover has ever driven on this rock type
tasks.gap: Texture and chemistry up close: nobody has ever had this rock in front of them
tasks.task: Abrade a patch and look inside (9 min) - the abrading bit with WATSON and SHERLOC (close-up camera, deep-UV Raman and fluorescence)

tasks.title: Elemental map of the fresh patch
tasks.stands_for: PIXL, micro X-ray fluorescence with a spot about a tenth of a millimetre wide
tasks.why: A map of which elements sit where tells you whether the rock is volcanic or was laid down in water.
tasks.where: The patch you just abraded, without moving the scale bar.
steps: Lay a grid over the close-up photo: a few millimetres across, ten by ten.
Work across the grid and note every change of colour or crystal shape, cell by cell.
Mark grains that look like salt, carbonate or clay. Those are the water-formed ones.
Write down whether the chemistry looks the same everywhere or comes in patches. Patches mean water moved through.
tasks.signal: No rover has ever driven on this rock type
tasks.gap: Texture and chemistry up close: nobody has ever had this rock in front of them
tasks.task: Elemental map of the fresh patch (4 min) - PIXL, micro X-ray fluorescence with a spot about a tenth of a millimetre wide

tasks.title: Take a sealed core
tasks.stands_for: the Mars 2020 coring bit and sample tubes
tasks.why: This is the only step that can ever be checked in a lab on Earth. Treat it as the point of the walk.
tasks.where: Within one arm length of the abraded patch, in Crater floor fractured 1 itself, never in a loose block.
steps: Core about 6 cm long and 1.3 cm wide, like a Mars 2020 tube, and keep it in one piece.
Seal the tube and label it: tube number, station, time, and which way was up.
Photograph the hole you left and the tube together, so the sample can never be mixed up.
Take one witness sample of the nearby air and dust, so contamination can be ruled out later.
Say the tube number on the radio and write it on the cuff.
tasks.source: Farley et al. 2020, Mars 2020 sampling and caching.
tasks.signal: No rover has ever driven on this rock type
tasks.gap: Texture and chemistry up close: nobody has ever had this rock in front of them
tasks.task: Take a sealed core (8 min) - the Mars 2020 coring bit and sample tubes

tasks.title: Read the contact
tasks.stands_for: classic field geology, the way Apollo crews worked a traverse
tasks.why: Order is time. Once you know which unit lies on the other, every sample from both gets an age order for free.
tasks.where: Walk the contact between Crater floor fractured 1 and Crater floor fractured rough until both are exposed within a few metres of each other.
steps: Photograph the contact from both sides, each time with the scale bar lying across the line.
Measure how the layers tilt: the compass direction they run and how steeply they dip.
Follow the contact about 20 m each way and note whether it stays straight, cuts across, or fades out.
Take one sample from each side of the Crater floor fractured 1 / Crater floor fractured rough line, within 2 m of it, labelled A (lower) and B (upper).
Write down which one you think is on top, and the one thing you saw that decided it.
tasks.source: Contacts from Stack et al. 2020, Jezero geologic map; field method after Apollo traverse geology.
tasks.signal: A mapped contact between two rock units runs through here
tasks.gap: Which rock sits on top of which, and therefore which one is older
tasks.task: Read the contact (12 min) IF TIME - classic field geology, the way Apollo crews worked a traverse

book:
MARSCUFF
Jezero EVA cuff

7.33 km walk
3:56 of 6:24 usable
FITS
No Point of No Return

HOW TO FOLLOW
WHITE = habitat.
PURPLE = stations.
RED = no return.
Glowing = route.
(beams in game,
pillars in the zip)

TIMELINE
0:00 Leave habitat
0:30 Arrive sta 1 (go by 5:55)
1:00 Leave sta 1
1:51 Arrive sta 2 (go by 5:54)
2:21 Leave sta 2
2:57 Arrive sta 3 (go by 5:54)
3:27 Leave sta 3
3:56 Back at habitat

AT THE HABITAT
Weather and dust log, 3 min
Do it before you leave and again when you get back.

WHERE
At the habitat, once before you leave and again when you get back.

STEPS
1. Note the time, the temperature, the wind direction and how hard it is blowing.
2. Look across the crater floor for dust devils and count them.
3. Photograph the sky to the north with the same exposure both times, so the haze can be compared.
4. If the view got hazier while you were out, say so. It changes how your pictures should be read.

STATION 1
Crater floor fractured 1
Arrive 0:30
Leave by 5:55

WHY HERE
- No rover has ever driven on this rock type. Texture and chemistry up close: nobody has ever had this rock in front of them
- A mapped contact between two rock units runs through here. Which rock sits on top of which, and therefore which one is older

STATION 1 JOBS
30 min must-do, 30 min booked, +12 if time
1. Station recon panorama (5 min)
2. Remote triage of three targets (4 min)
3. Abrade a patch and look inside (9 min)
4. Elemental map of the fresh patch (4 min)
5. Take a sealed core (8 min)
6. Read the contact (12 min) IF TIME
